odrang@nvidia.com
Please investigate the existing implementation of lldp.  Someone added it recently elsewhere.

yes, currently we have enabled LLDP service in OpenBMC, where EmitLLDP D-bus property on xyz.openbmc_project.Network.EthernetInterface allows enable/disable transmit/Emit LLDP packets on BMC ethernet interfaces.

please check these commits
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/openbmc/+/75749
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/phosphor-networkd/+/76368

I understand that this proposal to add support for both Trasmit and receive LLDP packets and completely enable LLDP data parsing on BMC and hosting on D-bus on each ethernet interfaces.

Patrick and Ravi, thanks you for the quick response.
Yes, Ravi this is correct.
The design adds support to control LLDP packets.
In transmit object we can both change and retrieve the content of the transmitted LLDP PDU.
In receive object we retrieve the content of the received LLDP PDU.
    
 I added more information about Emit LLDP in Background and References
section. 

Also added more explanation in the Operation section.

It seems like you've deleted entire sections out of the design document template.  Please restore them and fill them out.  We have a design document template for a reason; I'm not reviewing this further.

can we please add more details on how do we refresh D-bus objects based on LLDP packets received from Peer system connected over each ethernet interfaces.
since LLDP packets received in periodic interval

1. does neighbor's LLDP object goes away if BMC fails to receive LLDP packets after lldp  TTL interval timeout?

2. how are you planning to refresh/manage created LLDP neighbor D-bus objects for each interface.
   Here is some cases:
   - Peer Device plugged out and plugged in another device 
   - Peer Device is powered off or stopped emitting LLDP packets 
   

3. Networkd already defined interface for neighbors, are you planning to leverage existing interfaces?
  https://github.com/openbmc/phosphor-dbus-interfaces/blob/master/yaml/xyz/openbmc_project/Network/Neighbor.interface.yaml

>how are you planning to refresh/manage created LLDP neighbor D-bus objects for each interface

+1

Patrick, I updated the missing sections.
Ravi, 
1. The neighbor object doesn't go away. The design doesn't include polling the lldpd daemon on each TTL interval. It polls it only when required by busctl get-property or set-property command. If the property is not available at that time, it can populate it with "unavailable" value. 
2.The objects are created on service bring up according to the configuration files. What you ask can be done by polling the lldpd daemon. I am not sure if that is necessary because the service is only of interest when accessed by busctrl commands. And then it polls the daemon anyway.
3. LLDP advertises both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. I didn't find an interface that provides both options.
I immediately see that "Alternatives" is missing.  Please follow the design document template.

@asmitk01@in.ibm.com, @raviteja28031990@gmail.com 
what is the use case for online refreshing of the D-bus objects?

say if neighbor objects are created on service bring up according to the configuration files,
Most of network connections dynamically changes after BMC is up and running then LLDP shows stale old entries which are no longer connected to BMC.
since LLDP anyways providing information in regular intervals, it would ideal to refresh LLDP D-bus objects as per LLDP packets data

I did not understand why its only of interest when accessed by busctl commands?

The D-BUS objects, don't store LLDP data. when any if their properties are queried (by busctl or right, any other interface to access D-BUS objects) they will in turn query lldpd. lldpd stores up to date neighbor data from the last received LLDP PDU.
(Invalidated after LLDP TTL if newer PDU was not received).
SO, the D-BUS will properties always return up to date data.
Done

We have a use case where we will need an object representation of the discovered neighbour on the BMC that hosts the neighbour IP for other apps to use it.

In that case, my thought is:
Whenever the service comes up, it should check for the LLDP packet, if any, then parse it and create DBus objects under respective interfaces. Then, poll for the LLDP packets in specific intervals:
    * If the neighbour BMC is disconnected/stops emitting LLDP packets, then the created dbus object should be deleted
    * If a new BMC is plugged in, then the LLDP DBUS object should be refreshed to reflect the latest data.

I have been working on this lately, and have pushed some changes to openbmc and networkd:
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/openbmc/+/83385
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/phosphor-networkd/+/83384 (Marked WIP)

I can modify it based on what we conclude here and once dbus interfaces are in.

I will add that to the design: 
* If the neighbour BMC is disconnected/stops emitting LLDP packets, then the created dbus object should be deleted
* If a new BMC is plugged in, then the LLDP DBUS object should be refreshed to reflect the latest data.

Regarding your changes, we prefer to implement a dedicated service. This is discussed in Alternatives Considered section. You prefer to implement it in networkd?
We can provide a reference code for a dedicated service.

Yes, I have changed my implementation to have a separate service as proposed in this design doc.

Will update the networkd commit with the changes.

I do agree that implementing in a dedicated LLDP service would be cleaner way.
@Asmitha please push your changes in separate D-bus service, lets create a sub directory under phosphor-networkd
@asmitk01@in.ibm.com are you planning to implement the entire desgin?

Not entirely. https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/phosphor-networkd/+/83719/4 -> This commit chain will have the proposed design implemented to an extent.
1. Create LLDP Service
2. Host Ethernet interfaces dbus object
3. Provide enable/disable lldp support for each interface
4. Parse incoming LLDP packet contents and update them in the dbus object
5. Periodic refresh of LLDP dbus objects
That seems like complete management of the DBus objects. What parts of the design are not covered specifically? I need to know what to cover in future tasks.

Well, mostly yes.
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/q/topic:%22LLDP+Neighbor+Discovery%22 This has the entire commits related to lldp.
One thing that is not covered is "runtime configuration of transmit TLV properties" (It's the 4th one in the commit chain)
Okay, so the runtime configuration will be added later.

@patrick@stwcx.xyz Deepak added me to the CLA / Gerrit Group.

While LLDP itself is small, splitting it into its own service adds minor additional memory overhead.

Instead, have you thought of embedding it in the existing networkd loop, keeping the proposed interfaces same, but hosting it inside networkd?

We considered adding LLDP to networkd, and it is certainly a possible solution. Using a separate service will be easier to maintain and extend without adding extra dependencies and complexity to networkd.
how do we associate LLDP objects to each ethernet interface?

For each interface <if_name> we create 2 objects, for transmit and receive
/xyz/OpenBMC_project/network/lldp/<if_name>/transmit
/xyz/OpenBMC_project/network/lldp/<if_name>/receive

When accessing the receive object it will retrieve the neighbor information of that interface from lldpd. So, the information will always be up to date with the neighbor that is currently connected.
Done
Done
Direct liblldpctl’s stable iterator API calls (to get lldp packets from the listening socket) avoids lldpcli subprocess parsing.
@asmitk01@in.ibm.com good point. I will update the design document to use liblldpctl
Done
@patrick@stwcx.xyz this is the Alternatives section
Acknowledged.  I'm not sure why I missed it before.
So it's not quite "none".  This adds a new daemon in phosphor-networkd, potentially more daemons running.  Are there any sercurity impacts of running an LLDP daemon?

Right, there will be small runtime and memory overhead. I will update this section.
Regarding security, we will use the same library lldpcli uses to control lldpd.
So, it is as secure as using lldpcli, which we will have to use if don't implement this service. 
This is another reason to keep service separated from networkd and not increase networkd's attack surface.

Why create a new object? Instead can the ethernet dbus object implement Settings interface? - This will simplify.

The new objects map exactly to Redfish specification. Also having all the properties under the same namespace makes it easier to maintain and use. An option we discussed before is to combine the setting with the TLV properties, but then having different settings to Rx and Tx is beyond Redfish specification.

Yes. But what i meant here was to make eth0 and eth1 objects (for example) implement settings interface (like below), instead of creating a separate object (/settings) for each ethernet interface.

'''
busctl introspect xyz.openbmc_project.LLDP /xyz/openbmc_project/network/lldp/eth1
xyz.openbmc_project.Network.LLDP.Settings interface -         -            -
.EnableLLDP                               property  b         false        emits-change writable
'''
Reference: https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/phosphor-networkd/+/84082

the objects are separated to /xyz/openbmc_project/network/lldp/eth1/transmit and /xyz/openbmc_project/network/lldp/eth1/receive. Each implements the TLVs interface. if they also implement the settings interface, it implies different enable / disable for ex and tx.

The tree looks something like:
'''
busctl tree xyz.openbmc_project.LLDP
└─ /xyz
  └─ /xyz/openbmc_project
    └─ /xyz/openbmc_project/network
      └─ /xyz/openbmc_project/network/lldp

The plan is to have privilege separation. This is best to be handles by a systemd service than runs before the lldpd service and created the lldpd user and group.
This is to be handled in the scope of lldpd bb files, so I didn't add it to this design document.

For example: 

# lldpd-setup-user.service
[Unit]
Description=Configure lldpd user
After=systemd-remount-fs.service
After=xyz.openbmc_project.User.Manager.service
Before=lldpd.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/lldpd-setup-user.sh
ExecStartPost=/bin/systemctl --no-reload disable lldpd-setup-user.service
RemainAfterExit=yes
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=30

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target


# lldpd-setup-user.sh
#!/bin/sh

#Script to ensure lldpd user and group exist

groupadd --system lldpd 2>/dev/null

#Create user if missing
if ! id lldpd >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    useradd --system -g lldpd --shell /bin/false lldpd 
fi
